Definition
Grouping similar data points together based on their features.

Unsupervised learning technique.
No predefined labels; the algorithm identifies natural
groupings.
Used for exploratory data analysis and pattern discovery.

Types of Clustering
Partitional Clustering: Divides data into non-overlapping
subsets (e.g., K-Means).
Hierarchical Clustering: Builds a tree of clusters (e.g.,
Agglomerative, Divisive).
Density-Based Clustering: Groups data based on density
(e.g., DBSCAN).
Model-Based Clustering: Assumes data is generated from a
mixture of distributions (e.g., Gaussian Mixture Models).

K-Means Clustering
Definition
A type of unsupervised learning used for unlabeled data.
Goal: Find groups in the data, with the number of groups
represented by K.
Algorithm:
Works iteratively to assign each data point to one of K groups.
Clusters data points based on feature similarity.
Results:
Centroids of the K clusters (used to label new data).
Labels for the training data (each point assigned to a single
cluster).

What is K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)?
Definition
KNN is a simple, non-parametric, supervised machine learning
algorithm used for both classification and regression tasks.
Key Characteristics:
Instance-based (Lazy) Learning: It does not build an
explicit internal model during a training phase. Instead, it
memorizes the training dataset.
Similarity Assumption: It operates on the premise that
similar things exist in close proximity to each other.
Supervised: Unlike K-Means (which clusters unlabeled data),
KNN requires labeled data to classify new observations.

The KNN Algorithm: Step-by-Step
To classify a new, unknown data point, the algorithm follows these
steps:
1. Choose K: Select the number of neighbors, K .
2. Calculate Distances: Compute the distance between the
new data point and every point in the training dataset.
3. Find Neighbors: Sort the distances in ascending order and
select the top K nearest data points.
4. Vote (Classification): Count the class labels of these K
neighbors.
5. Assign Class: Assign the new data point to the class that
appears most frequently (majority vote).

Choosing the Right K
Selecting K is crucial for model performance:
Small K (e.g., K = 1 ): High variance, low bias. The model
perfectly fits the training data but is highly sensitive to noise
and outliers (Overfitting).
Large K : Low variance, high bias. The decision boundaries
become smoother, but it may ignore localized patterns
(Underfitting).
Best Practices for K
Choose an odd number for K to avoid tie votes in binary
classification.

A common rule of thumb is K = N , where N is the
number of data points.
Use cross-validation to test different K values and select the
one with the lowest error rate.

• Requirements need to be evolved to reflect this changed problem.

hardware or update of existing hardware; introduction of new regulations which
require system compliance.
• Funders and users of the systems are usually different – end-user requirements are
not fully implemented due to budgetary constraints.

chunks.title: Requirements Validation for HPMS
chunks.text:
Requirements Validation for HPMS
• To validate functional requirements, you can use several techniques such as reviews ,
walkthroughs , prototyping , and user acceptance testing (UAT) .
• To validate non-functional requirements, you can use a mix of performance testing ,
security audits , and usability testing.
26

chunks.label: 第 27 页
chunks.title: Validation of Functional Requirements – 1
chunks.text:
Validation of Functional Requirements – 1
• Patient Registration (FR1)
• Test Case : Ensure that the registration form accepts all required fields, such as full
name, date of birth, address, and medical history.
• Validation Method :
• Static Analysis : Verify that the form fields match the expected data types (e.g.,
name as string, DOB as date, medical history as text).
• Dynamic Analysis : Conduct a usability test where hospital staff attempt to
register new patients. Check if the unique patient ID is generated correctly and if
the confirmation message is displayed.
• Boundary Testing : Test the form with valid and invalid inputs (e.g., empty fields,
invalid dates, etc.).
27

chunks.label: 第 28 页
chunks.title: Validation of Functional Requirements – 2
chunks.text:
Validation of Functional Requirements – 2
• Appointment Scheduling (FR2) :
• Test Case : Ensure that the system prevents double-booking and schedules
appointments only during available time slots.
• Validation Method :
• Simulate Multiple Users : Test if the system correctly checks for doctor
availability by attempting to schedule overlapping appointments.
• Cross-check with Real-World Data : Validate against actual available doctor
schedules and ensure appointments are scheduled correctly.
• User Acceptance Testing (UAT) : Hospital staff should test scheduling, ensuring
that the interface is intuitive and functions as expected.
28

chunks.label: 第 29 页
chunks.title: Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 1
chunks.text:
Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 1
• Performance :
• Test Case : Validate that the system can handle 1000 concurrent users without
significant degradation in performance.
• Validation Method : Conduct load testing to simulate the specified number of users
(NF1) and measure response times, database queries, and system resource usage.
Check that the system can handle the load within acceptable parameters (e.g., 95%
of requests load within 3 seconds (NF2) ).
29

chunks.label: 第 30 页
chunks.title: Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 2
chunks.text:
Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 2
• Usability :
• Test Case : Ensure that the user interface is intuitive and easy to navigate.
• Validation Method :
• Usability Testing (NF3) : Perform usability tests with hospital staff (target users)
to evaluate the interface. Record user satisfaction (satisfaction rate over 90%),
the time it takes to complete common tasks, and error rates.
• Accessibility Testing (NF4) : Ensure that the system is accessible by users on both
desktop and mobile devices (e.g. produce the same outputs).
30

chunks.label: 第 31 页
chunks.title: Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 3
chunks.text:
Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 3
• Security :
• Test Case : Validate that the system implements strong authentication and data
encryption.
• Validation Method :
• Penetration Testing (NF5) : Conduct penetration tests to check for
vulnerabilities, such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and insecure
APIs.
• Encryption Testing (NF6) : Verify that patient data is encrypted during
transmission (SSL/TLS) and when stored in the database.
• Access Control Review (NF7) : Check if users can only access data they are
authorized to see (e.g., nurses can’t access billing information).
31

chunks.label: 第 32 页
chunks.title: Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 4
chunks.text:
Validation of Non-Functional Requirements – 4
• Reliability :
• Test Case : Ensure the system has 99.9% uptime annually and that backups occur
daily.
• Validation Method :
• Availability Testing (NF8) : Simulate system failures and verify that the system
recovers within the specified time.
• Backup Verification (NF9) : Test backup processes to ensure data is recoverable
and complete.
32

chunks.label: 第 33 页
chunks.title: Validation of System Interfaces – 1
chunks.text:
Validation of System Interfaces – 1
• Database Interface :
• Test Case : Ensure that the database schema supports the system's functionality and
retrieves data correctly.
• Validation Method :
• SQL Query Validation : Execute SQL queries that reflect actual use cases (e.g.,
retrieving patient details or appointment schedules) and ensure the correct
results are returned.
• Consistency Check : Verify that all data inserted into the database matches the
schema definition (e.g., Patient ID is numeric, Date of Birth is in date format).
33

chunks.label: 第 34 页
chunks.title: Validation of System Interfaces – 2
chunks.text:
Validation of System Interfaces – 2
• External Interfaces :
• Test Case : Ensure integration with external services like insurance providers and
email/SMS services works as expected.
• Validation Method :
• API Testing : Test API endpoints to confirm that data is sent and received
correctly from third-party systems (e.g., insurance validation APIs, email/SMS
notifications).
• Integration Testing : Simulate a complete workflow where a patient's insurance
is validated, and an appointment notification is sent to the patient, ensuring that
the entire system is functioning correctly.
34

chunks.label: 第 35 页
chunks.title: Validation of Product Features (Use Case)
chunks.text:
Validation of Product Features (Use Case)
• Use Case Validation :
• Test Case : Validate that all use cases work as expected and cover all possible user
interactions.
• Validation Method :
• End-User Testing : Test the system by simulating real-world workflows, such as
registering a patient and scheduling an appointment, to ensure the system
behaves according to the use case descriptions.
35

chunks.label: 第 36 页
chunks.title: Validation of Assumptions and Dependencies
chunks.text:
Validation of Assumptions and Dependencies
• Assumptions :
• Test Case : Validate assumptions such as the hospital having reliable internet or staff
having basic computer literacy.
• Validation Method :
• Environment Simulation : Check the system’s performance under conditions
where the internet connection is slow or unreliable.
• Training Materials : Confirm that training materials or tutorials are provided for
users who might not be familiar with the system.
36

chunks.label: 第 37 页
chunks.title: Validation of Assumptions and Dependencies
chunks.text:
Validation of Assumptions and Dependencies
• Dependencies :
• Test Case : Validate that external systems (e.g., email/SMS service) and the database
are available and functioning.
• Validation Method :
• Dependency Testing : Simulate the failure of an external service (e.g., email/SMS
service down) and check how the system handles the situation (e.g., retry
mechanism, error notification).
37

Branching and Control flow
• So far, all instructions learnt allow us to
manipulate data.
• So we’ve built a calculator.
• In order to build a computer, we need the ability
to make decisions…
• Branching and Control flow
• Branch instruction affect the Program Counter
(PC) and hence the control flow of the program
• Conditional branch instructions perform a branch
depending on a condition.
• Unconditional branch instructions (e.g. goto )
perform a branch unconditionally.

chunks.label: 第 6 页
chunks.title: Control Flow in High Level Languages
chunks.text:
Control Flow in High Level Languages
• goto has (mostly) been eliminated from high level programming
languages
 It will lead to an unmaintainable mess
• Structured statements: if , if/else , while and for are used instead
• But in MIPS, both types of branching ( goto and if - family) are
provided. We will learn MIPS branching instructions that
correspond to the above structs.

chunks.label: 第 7 页
chunks.title: MIPS Branch Instructions
chunks.text:
MIPS Branch Instructions
• beq a, b, L - Branch on equal
 Go to instruction at label L if a==b , otherwise, continue with the next
instruction
• bne a, b, L - Branch on not equal
 Go to instruction at label L if a!=b , otherwise, continue with the next
instruction
• j L – Jump to
 jump to the instruction at label L

chunks.label: 第 8 页
chunks.title: Conditional Branching ( beq )
chunks.text:
Conditional Branching ( beq )
# MIPS assembly
addi $s0, $0, 4 # $s0 = 0 + 4 = 4
addi $s1, $0, 1 # $s1 = 0 + 1 = 1
sll $s1, $s1, 2 # $s1 = 1 << 2 = 4
beq $s0, $s1, target # branch is taken
addi $s1, $s1, 1 # not executed
sub $s1, $s1, $s0 # not executed
target : # label
add $s1, $s1, $s0 # $s1 = 4 + 4 = 8
Labels indicate instruction locations in a program. They cannot
use reserve words and must be followed by a colon (:).

chunks.label: 第 9 页
chunks.title: Conditional Branching ( bne )
chunks.text:
Conditional Branching ( bne )
# MIPS assembly
addi $s0, $0, 4 # $s0 = 0 + 4 = 4
addi $s1, $0, 1 # $s1 = 0 + 1 = 1
sll $s1, $s1, 2 # $s1 = 1 << 2 = 4
bne $s0, $s1, target # branch if not equal
addi $s1, $s1, 1 # $s1 = 4 + 1 = 5

chunks.label: 第 17 页
chunks.title: Inequality in MIPS
chunks.text:
Inequality in MIPS
• Until now, we’ve only tested equalities ( beq and bne ), but general
programs need to test ‘<’ and ‘>’
• Set on Less Than:
 slt rd , rs , rt
 if ( rs < rt) rd = 1 ; else rd = 0 ;
 slti rt, rs , constant
 if ( rs < constant) rt = 1 ; else rt = 0 ;
Compile by hand: if (g < h) goto Less;
Let g: $s0, h: $s1
slt $t0,$s0,$s1 # $t0 = 1 if g<h
bne $t0,$0,Less # goto Less if $t0 !=$0 （ $t0=1 ）

chunks.label: 第 18 页
chunks.title: Branch Instruction Design
chunks.text:
Branch Instruction Design
• MIPS has no “branch on less than”, i.e., blt , bge . Why?
• Hardware for <, ≥, … are slower than =, ≠
• Combining with branch involves more work per instruction,
requiring a slower clock
• All instructions penalized!
• Although beq and bne are less direct (need to combine with slt ),
this is a good design compromise between performance and code
efficiency.

chunks.label: 第 19 页
chunks.title: Signed vs. Unsigned ‘ slt ’
chunks.text:
Signed vs. Unsigned ‘ slt ’
• Signed comparison: slt , slti
• Unsigned comparison: sltu , sltui
• Example
• $s0 = 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111
• $s1 = 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0001
slt $t0, $s0, $s1 # signed
• – 1 < +1 , so $t0 = 1
sltu $t0, $s0, $s1 # unsigned
• +4,294,967,295 > +1 , so $t0 = 0

chunks.label: 第 24 页
chunks.title: Accessing Array Data in MIPS
chunks.text:
Accessing Array Data in MIPS
• Since arrays can store lots of data, and we have only a small (~32)
number of registers, it is infeasible to use the registers for long -
term storage of the array data
• Hence, arrays are stored in the data segment of a MIPS program
• E.g. the declaration of an array with 8 words is:
arr : .word 3, 10, 4, 1, 15, 9, 2, 6
• To access the data in the array requires that we know the address
of the data and then use the load word ( lw ) or store word ( sw )
instructions

chunks.label: 第 25 页

Accessing Array Data in MIPS
arr : .word 3, 10, 4, 15, 5, 9, 2, 6
• To find where the array is: la $t0, arr
 $t0 contains the address of the first element '3' in the array
 The index address of the second word ‘10’ is $t0 + 4
 The address of the fifth word ‘5’ is $t0 + 16
• The following code will place the value of arr [6] into the $t4 :
la $t3, arr # put address of arr into $t3
li $t2, 6 # put the index into $t2
sll $t2, $t2, 2 # 4x the index to find the byte location
add $t1, $t2, $t3 # obtain the address
lw $t4, 0($t1) # get the value from the array cell

• Contracts : uses less memory when the space is no longer needed
• Grows down (from higher to lower memory addresses)
• Stack pointer: $ sp , points to top of the stack

• Response time

 The actual time the CPU spends computing a specific task
 Does not include time spent waiting for I/O or running other
programs
 Can be further divided into
 User CPU time: the CPU time spent in a program itself
 System CPU time: the CPU time spent in the OS performing tasks on behalf

performance n is
n = Performance_X / Performance_Y
= Execution_Time_Y / Execution_Time_X

cases.question: What are the three main topics covered in Lecture 7 of COMP1037?
cases.referenceAnswer: The three main topics covered in Lecture 7 are Regression, Classification, and Overfitting and Underfitting.

cases.question: What is the mathematical form of the L2 loss function as defined in the lecture?
cases.referenceAnswer: The L2 loss function is defined as L(y, f(x)) = (y − f(x))².

cases.question: According to the lecture, what is the key assumption underlying Naive Bayes?
cases.referenceAnswer: Naive Bayes assumes feature independence given the class — i.e., P(x₁, x₂ | Y) = P(x₁ | Y) P(x₂ | Y).

cases.question: In the coffee shop revenue example on page 13–14, what is the fitted linear model y̅ = θ̂₀ + θ̂₁x, and what are the estimated parameters?
cases.referenceAnswer: The fitted model is y̅ = 2x; thus θ̂₀ = 0 and θ̂₁ = 2.

cases.question: What does the design matrix X and response vector y look like in the coffee shop revenue example with data points {(1,2), (2,4), (3,6)}?
cases.referenceAnswer: The design matrix X is [[1,1],[1,2],[1,3]] and the response vector y is [2,4,6]ᵀ.

cases.question: In the Naive Bayes email spam example (page 26), what is the full training dataset table showing features x₁ ('free'), x₂ ('win'), and class labels?
cases.referenceAnswer: Email 1: x₁=yes, x₂=yes, Class=Spam; Email 2: x₁=yes, x₂=no, Class=Spam; Email 3: x₁=no, x₂=yes, Class=Not Spam; Email 4: x₁=no, x₂=no, Class=Not Spam.

cases.question: Why is the term P(X) (the evidence) unnecessary for classification decisions in Naive Bayes, according to the lecture?
cases.referenceAnswer: Because P(X) is the same for all classes, it acts as a normalizing constant and does not affect which class has the larger posterior probability.

cases.question: How does L2 loss differ from L1 loss in terms of sensitivity to outliers, according to the lecture?
cases.referenceAnswer: L2 loss is quadratic in residuals and thus gives high weight to outlying points, whereas L1 loss is more robust in the presence of outliers.

cases.question: Compare the decision boundaries of logistic regression and decision trees as described in the lecture.
cases.referenceAnswer: Logistic regression produces a linear decision boundary (a hyperplane), while decision trees produce rectangular decision boundaries by splitting along feature axes.

cases.question: What is the exact value of the regularization parameter λ used in the regularized loss function shown on page 39?
cases.referenceAnswer: The lecture does not specify a numerical value for λ; it only introduces λ as a generic penalty coefficient in the regularized loss formula.

cases.question: What are the three main types of unsupervised learning discussed in Lecture 9?
cases.referenceAnswer: Clustering, Dimensionality Reduction, and Association Rule Learning.

cases.question: According to the课件, what is the objective function minimized in K-means clustering, and what do μ_i and ||x − μ_i||² represent?
cases.referenceAnswer: The objective function minimized is J(C, μ) = ∑_{i=1}^k ∑_{x ∈ C_i} ||x − μ_i||², where μ_i is the centroid of cluster C_i and ||x − μ_i||² is the squared Euclidean distance between data point x and centroid μ_i.

cases.question: What are the four steps of the KNN classification algorithm as described in the课件?
cases.referenceAnswer: 1. Choose K; 2. Calculate distances between the new data point and every training point; 3. Find the K nearest neighbors by sorting distances; 4. Vote (count class labels of K neighbors); 5. Assign the new point to the most frequent class.

cases.question: What are two key limitations of K-Means clustering listed in the课件?
cases.referenceAnswer: It is sensitive to initial centroid positions, and it requires the number of clusters to be specified in advance.

cases.question: What does the figure on page 18 illustrate about centroid updates in K-Means?
cases.referenceAnswer: It shows that for each cluster, a new centroid is calculated by taking the mean position of all points in the cluster, and arrows indicate the change in centroid positions.

cases.question: What does the PCA visualization on pages 43–48 demonstrate about axis reorientation and dimensionality reduction?
cases.referenceAnswer: It demonstrates reorienting axes to be centered on the data and parallel to the direction of maximum variance, allowing compression of a two-dimensional dataset into one dimension by discarding the axis with minimal variance.

cases.question: Based on the课件, why is feature scaling (normalization/standardization) required for KNN?
cases.referenceAnswer: KNN is sensitive to irrelevant features due to the curse of dimensionality, and requires feature scaling to ensure all features contribute equally to distance calculations.

cases.question: How does supervised learning differ from unsupervised learning in terms of data requirements and primary goals, according to the comparison table on page 6?
cases.referenceAnswer: Supervised learning uses labeled data and aims to predict outcomes, whereas unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data and aims to discover patterns.

cases.question: Contrast K-Means and KNN with respect to supervision, training behavior, and data labeling requirements.
cases.referenceAnswer: K-Means is unsupervised and operates on unlabeled data; KNN is supervised and requires labeled data. K-Means builds clusters iteratively via centroid updates; KNN is an instance-based (lazy) learner that memorizes training data without building an explicit model.

cases.question: What is the exact time complexity of the K-means algorithm in terms of n (number of data points), k (number of clusters), d (dimensions), and i (iterations)?
cases.referenceAnswer: The课件 does not specify the time complexity formula for K-means.

cases.question: What is the central organizing principle of object-oriented programming according to this lecture?
cases.referenceAnswer: Code is organized around data.

cases.question: According to the lecture, what is the role of a constructor in Java?
cases.referenceAnswer: A constructor initializes an object when it is created.

cases.question: What happens to an object in Java when no references point to it?
cases.referenceAnswer: It becomes eligible for garbage collection.

cases.question: Why does the lecture state that using a method like range() is better than computing car.mpg * car.fuelCap directly in client code?
cases.referenceAnswer: It encapsulates behavior and hides implementation details from the user; callers need not know how range is computed.

cases.question: In the 'A common bug' code snippet on page 25, what is printed by showData() after calling setData(10, 20)?

cases.question: Summarize the key difference between procedural and object-oriented programming as presented in the lecture.
cases.referenceAnswer: Procedural programming organizes programs as sequences of instructions focused on 'what to do step by step', while object-oriented programming organizes programs as objects that combine data and behavior, focusing on 'who owns the data and what they can do'.

cases.question: Compare how assignment works for primitive types versus reference types in Java, based on the lecture examples.
cases.referenceAnswer: For primitive types, assignment copies the value; for reference types, assignment copies the address/reference (not the object).

cases.question: How does the 'no-parameter constructor' (page 23) differ from the 'constructor with parameters' (page 24) in terms of flexibility and initialization control?
cases.referenceAnswer: The no-parameter constructor always initializes fields with fixed values (e.g., fuelCap = 14), whereas the parameterized constructor allows caller-specified initialization (e.g., new Vehicle(14, 12, 4)), making it more flexible.

cases.question: What is the time complexity of Java's garbage collector algorithm as described in this lecture?
cases.referenceAnswer: The lecture does not specify or describe the time complexity of Java's garbage collector algorithm.

cases.question: What is the primary purpose of requirements validation according to the lecture?
cases.referenceAnswer: The primary purpose of requirements validation is to check that the requirements define the system that the customer really wants.

cases.question: According to the lecture, what are the five types of checks performed during a formal requirements review?
cases.referenceAnswer: The five types of checks are: validity checks, consistency checks, completeness checks, realism checks, and verifiability checks.

cases.question: Why is fixing a requirements problem after deployment more costly than fixing design or coding errors?
cases.referenceAnswer: Because the cost of fixing a requirements problem by making a system change is usually greater than repairing design or coding errors.

cases.question: According to the lecture, what is the key benefit of conducting internal requirements validation before external validation?
cases.referenceAnswer: The key benefit is that it serves as a practice run — if you can explain the full requirements, time plan, and requested budget clearly to your team and manager without trouble, then you are ready to present to the client.

cases.question: How does internal requirements validation differ from external requirements validation, based on the lecture material?
cases.referenceAnswer: Internal validation involves presenting requirements to 'boss and colleagues' (e.g., manager, developer, quality manager) as a first sanity check; external validation involves presenting back to participants/clients/users to confirm agreement with the understanding and prioritization.

cases.question: Compare the roles of prototyping and test-case generation as requirements validation techniques, according to the lecture.
cases.referenceAnswer: Prototyping involves developing an executable model of the system to let end-users and customers experience and provide feedback on their needs and expectations; test-case generation involves developing tests from user requirements before coding (e.g., test-driven development) to verify testability — if a test is difficult or impossible to design, it signals problematic requirements.

cases.question: How does the lecture distinguish Agile Retrospectives from Agile Postmortems in terms of timing, ownership, and purpose?

cases.question: What is the purpose of the 'slt' instruction in MIPS, and how does it set its destination register?
cases.referenceAnswer: The 'slt' instruction performs a signed 'set on less than' operation: if the first source register is less than the second source register, it sets the destination register to 1; otherwise, it sets it to 0.

cases.question: Why does MIPS not provide direct branch-on-less-than instructions (e.g., 'blt') according to the课件?
cases.referenceAnswer: Because hardware for '<', '≥', etc. is slower than for '=', '≠', and combining comparison with branching would require more work per instruction, penalizing the clock speed of all instructions.

cases.question: In the MIPS procedure calling convention, which registers are designated as callee-saved, and why must they be preserved by the callee?
cases.referenceAnswer: Callee-saved registers are $s0–$s7, $ra, and $sp. They must be preserved because the caller may have used them, and the callee must avoid unintended side effects on the caller's state.

cases.question: In the code example on page 8, what is the final value of $s1 after execution completes, and which instructions are skipped due to the 'beq' branch?

Summarize the key responsibilities of the caller and callee in the MIPS procedure calling convention, as stated in the Summary section (page 43) and elaborated in earlier pages.
cases.referenceAnswer: The caller is responsible for passing arguments in $a0–$a3, making the call with jal, and managing caller-saved registers ($t0–$t9, $v0–$v1, $a0–$a3) if needed. The callee is responsible for preserving callee-saved registers ($s0–$s7, $ra, $sp), performing the task, returning the result in $v0/$v1, and restoring saved registers before returning with jr $ra.

cases.question: Compare the branching logic used in translating the high-level 'if (i == j)' statement (page 13) versus the 'while (pow != 128)' loop (page 15): how do their MIPS implementations differ in terms of condition testing, and what is the common pattern?
cases.referenceAnswer: Both translate by testing the *opposite* condition: 'if (i == j)' uses 'bne $s3, $s4, L1' to skip the body when false, and 'while (pow != 128)' uses 'beq $s0, $t0, done' to exit the loop when the termination condition is met. The common pattern is that MIPS conditional branches are used to jump *around* the block (skip it) rather than jump *into* it — i.e., they implement 'branch if condition fails'.

cases.question: Contrast the use of 'j' (page 10) and 'jr' (page 11) instructions: what type of operand does each take, and how does that affect their flexibility?
cases.referenceAnswer: 'j' takes a label (immediate address) as operand and performs an unconditional jump to that fixed location. 'jr' takes a register (e.g., $s0) as operand and jumps to the address stored in that register, enabling dynamic/indirect jumps (e.g., return addresses, function pointers).

cases.question: According to the课件, what does 'CPU execution time' (or 'CPU time') specifically exclude that 'response time' includes?
cases.referenceAnswer: CPU execution time excludes time spent waiting for I/O or running other programs, whereas response time includes all aspects such as disk accesses, memory accesses, I/O activities, and CPU time.

cases.question: What are the two components that determine the average CPI (Clock Cycles per Instruction), according to the课件?
cases.referenceAnswer: The average CPI is determined by the weighted sum across instruction classes: the sum over i of (CPI_i × Instruction_Count_i / Total_Instruction_Count).

cases.question: What three factors appear in the classic CPU performance equation for CPU Time, and how are they related?
cases.referenceAnswer: CPU Time = Instruction Count × CPI × Clock Period. Alternatively, CPU Time = (Instruction Count × CPI) / Clock Rate.

cases.question: Based on the CPI Example on page 14, compute the ratio of CPU Time_B to CPU Time_A — show the numeric substitution using the given values.
In the CPU Time Example on page 11, what arithmetic steps are shown to derive Clock Rate_B = 4GHz? List the key substitutions and simplifications.
cases.referenceAnswer: Clock Rate_B = Clock Cycles_B / CPU Time_B; Clock Cycles_B = 1.2 × Clock Cycles_A; Clock Cycles_A = CPU Time_A × Clock Rate_A = 10s × 2GHz = 20 × 10⁹; so Clock Cycles_B = 1.2 × 20 × 10⁹ = 24 × 10⁹; then Clock Rate_B = (24 × 10⁹) / 6s = 4 × 10⁹ Hz = 4GHz.

cases.question: Summarize the four fundamental components of CPU performance listed in the 'Performance Summary' table on page 18, including their units of measure.
cases.referenceAnswer: CPU execution time for a program (seconds), Instruction count (instructions executed), Clock cycles per instruction (CPI) (average number of clock cycles per instruction), Clock cycle time (period) (seconds per clock cycle).

cases.question: Compare how replacing the processor with a faster version versus adding more processors affects response time and throughput, based solely on page 3.
cases.referenceAnswer: Replacing the processor with a faster version improves both response time and throughput; adding more processors improves throughput but does not improve response time for a single task.

cases.question: Compare the eigenvalue detection process for ℝ→ℝ endomorphisms (page 7) versus ℝ²→ℝ² endomorphisms (pages 8–9 and 20–21). What makes the former trivial and the latter nontrivial?

cases.question: How does the eigenspace structure differ between the eigenvalue λ = −1 in the ℝ²→ℝ² example on page 16 and the eigenvalue λ = 2 in the ℝ³→ℝ³ example on page 28?
